title: SLA degradation and traffic steering intake with Nyx Communications
summary: Discovery focused on how Redwood handles tiered degradation (soft vs hard SLOs), traffic steering across regions, and suitability of hosted vs dedicated vs private for Nyx's low-latency comms use case. Key asks: deterministic behavior under partial outages, audit trails for fallbacks, and pricing impact expectations. Agreed next steps: run a 2-day benchmark, share security docs, and provide cost delta scenarios for partial-degradation SLOs.
topics: SLA degradation modes (soft degrade, partial capacity, circuit-breaker)
Multi-region traffic steering and geo-priority policies
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private suitability & tradeoffs
Observability and audit logs for fallback events
action_items: Alex Monroe: Send hosted/dedicated/private pricing matrix and sample contracts (due 2026-04-16)
Priya Shah: Draft a benchmark plan (2-day, synthetic load, KV cache priming, lat/99, error-rate) and share runbook (due 2026-04-17)
Carlos Ruiz: Provide representative traffic profile and sensitive-region list for pilot (due 2026-04-16)
Maya Lin: Confirm internal stakeholders and calendar availability for pilot week (due 2026-04-20)
next_steps: Schedule 2-day pilot in sandbox with dedicated capacity on one region + hosted fallback
Share SOC2 + network diagrams + KMS/HSM questionnaire from Redwood security pack
Priya to run a quick P50/P95/P99 profile simulation and return results
Alex to provide cost delta examples for 1% vs 5% allowable degradation in SLA
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we uh we really appreciate the time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya, our systems engineer.
[00:00:10] Priya Shah: hi all, i'll be covering the technical questions about routing and degrade modes.
[00:00:15] Maya Lin: Thanks Alex, thanks Priya. Quick intro — I'm Maya, CTO at Nyx. With me Carlos our SRE and Leah product who owns latency SLAs.
[00:00:27] Carlos Ruiz: hey. real quick we run a low-latency routing mesh for chat and voice transcriptions, p50 target 40ms, p99 under 250ms — av load varies 7k rps at peak.
[00:00:40] Alex Monroe: Got it. So main discussion today is around how Redwood can behave under partial failures — circuit breakers, traffic steering, multi-region fallback, that sort of thing.
[00:00:48] Leah Patel: yes and we want to understand cost impact when we intentionally let quality degrade vs spinning more capacity.
[00:00:55] Priya Shah: to frame the options quickly: hosted gives fastest time to value but it's multitenant and we provide automated region fallback policies; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and you can choose autoscale policies; private (VPC/on-prem) gives isolation and direct network control but is heavier ops. Each has different failure modes and tradeoffs.
[00:01:12] Maya Lin: Can you explain what you mean by "degrade modes" — we have internal categories: soft degrade where latency goes up a bit, hard degrade where model quality is reduced, and total fallback to a smaller model.
[00:01:22] Priya Shah: yeah exactly. We typically implement three levers: traffic shedding (reject/new-requests), model-graceful-degrade (route to a smaller quantized model or 8-bit variant), and region-steering (send traffic to a healthy region). There are also prefix/KV cache priming considerations — cold caches can blow up your p99.
[00:01:40] Carlos Ruiz: when you say route to a smaller model — is that automatic? how deterministic is the decision path? we need reproducible behavior for audits.
[00:01:50] Priya Shah: decision paths are policy driven. You can create a policy like: if p99>300ms for 2 minutes then switch to model-x-8q or route 60% to other-region. Policies are versioned and we keep audit logs of decisions and rollbacks. In hosted we keep the control plane; in dedicated we can give you the private control plane option so logs feed into your SIEM.
[00:02:10] Maya Lin: audit logs are critical. Can you retain full fallback decision events for six months?
[00:02:17] Alex Monroe: standard retention for hosted audit events is 90 days, enterprise packages can extend to 12 months. For dedicated/private we can negotiate longer retention and S3 export hooks.
[00:02:27] Leah Patel: that retention delta impacts cost and compliance. We'll need the exportable raw events.
[00:02:31] Priya Shah: yep, we have structured events: trigger, metric snapshot, model selected, request hash. We can export to your bucket. Sometimes the S3 path names are slightly different in the transcript — oh sorry, that's me thinking out loud.
[00:02:45] Carlos Ruiz: talk to me about geo-priority. We have EU customers and US customers and some APAC. We need strict data residency — EU requests must never leave eu-west-1. How does Redwood enforce region affinity?
[00:02:57] Priya Shah: you can pin routes by country/region, and set hard affinity: if eu request arrives and eu region is degraded you can choose between (a) block / return fail, (b) fallback within region to quantized smaller model, or (c) route to other-eu region. We treat data residency as a first-class policy.
[00:03:15] Maya Lin: So option (b) is what we might want — degrade quality in-region rather than send data outside. Does that work with hosted?
[00:03:21] Alex Monroe: hosted supports in-region fallbacks where available; we also maintain verified model variants per region. The main thing is capacity — if entire region is out we need to choose policy that fits your compliance needs.
[00:03:32] Carlos Ruiz: what's the fail-open/close default? like if control plane loses heartbeat do requests keep flowing?
[00:03:38] Priya Shah: default is fail-safe: we keep worker-plane decisions local for short windows, but we drop non-critical control updates. For long-term control-plane loss the behavior depends on deploy mode — dedicated with private control retains more local autonomy. There's cached policy TTL.
[00:03:54] Leah Patel: how do circuit breakers surface to our dashboards? we need events and reason codes.
[00:04:00] Priya Shah: every circuit breaker change emits an event with reason code (metric, absolute error thresholds, latency window). Redwood Console surfaces them per-route and per-model and you can wire those events to Slack/PagerDuty or export them.
[00:04:10] Alex Monroe: quick note — those reason codes are human readable but also machine friendly for your incident playbooks.
[00:04:16] Maya Lin: On the topic of cost — can you give an example: if we allow a 5% permitted degradation in p99, what cost savings might we expect versus maintaining hard SLOs?
[00:04:26] Priya Shah: ballpark: with intelligent batching, cache reuse, and model-variant steering a 5% accepted deg can reduce token-cost by ~12-22% depending on workload. We'll need your traffic shape and prompt lengths for precise numbers.
[00:04:40] Carlos Ruiz: we'll share traffic profiles after the call. Also — we prefer reserved capacity during our highest 4 hours of the day and burst to hosted for spikes. Is that supported?
[00:04:50] Alex Monroe: yes that's essentially Dedicated + burst to Hosted policy. We call it a mixed-mode routing — dedicated pool handles baseline, traffic governor allows burst to shared capacity with cost controls. You can set a hard limit on burst.
[00:05:02] Leah Patel: if we do burst to hosted, how is data handled? we need encryption in transit and at rest, and keys managed by our KMS.
[00:05:10] Priya Shah: hosted supports TLS in transit; for at-rest KMS integration we provide envelope encryption and optional customer-managed keys (CMK) in supported clouds. For end-to-end control and HSM you should look at Private.
[00:05:22] Maya Lin: Priya, you mentioned KV cache priming — practically how much does a cold cache hurt latency?
[00:05:28] Priya Shah: it depends. On warm caches P50 is dominated by model decode; a cold KV prefix miss can multiply p99 by 3–5x during priming. We recommend pre-warming prefixes for expected flows; Redwood Optimize can suggest priming and cache TTLs.
[00:05:43] Carlos Ruiz: okay that explains some of our spikes. For the pilot we want a scenario: 2-day run, one region dedicated baseline, second region hosted fallback, synthetic ramp to 7k rps, run model fallback policies and capture metrics and audit logs.
[00:05:56] Alex Monroe: that aligns with our standard pilot template. We'll need your traffic traces and a list of 'sensitive' geo rules.
[00:06:02] Maya Lin: sensitive geo rules = EU-in-region only, APAC prefer but fall back to apac-neighbor, US can failover to us-west.
[00:06:10] Priya Shah: noted. For the pilot we'll instrument p50/p95/p99, error-rate, tokens-per-request, and 'fallback rate' — percent of requests that hit a fallback path. We'll also capture cost-per-1k-tokens for each policy.
[00:06:22] Leah Patel: how quickly can you provision dedicated baseline for pilot? we have a narrow window two weeks from now.
[00:06:27] Alex Monroe: we can provision reserved capacity for a short pilot within 3–5 business days given region availability. We'll confirm once Priya drafts the size.
[00:06:35] Carlos Ruiz: what about SLA language — do you have degrade clauses? we need something that reflects partial degradation tolerances.
[00:06:42] Alex Monroe: standard SLAs cover uptime and per-request latency baselines; for partial degradation we include explicit clauses that define allowable fallback windows and associated credits. The legal team can draft a tailored exhibit for degradation tiers (e.g., allowable 1% hard-degrade, 5% soft-degrade monthly).
[00:06:56] Maya Lin: And billing adjustments for those credits — is it pro rata?
[00:07:00] Alex Monroe: yes typically pro rata, defined in the contract exhibit. We'll surface sample language.
[00:07:05] Priya Shah: small technical point: when modelling degradation economics we look at two axes: compute cost saved and user-impacted fallback rate. Sometimes saving 10% compute but increasing fallback rate by 20% is unacceptable. So the evaluation must include user-visible metrics.
[00:07:19] Leah Patel: interesting — so the product-team view matters. We'll include user-impact thresholds in the pilot success criteria.
[00:07:24] Carlos Ruiz: another question: in Dedicated if the control plane is out, what's the TTL for policy decisions? i.e. how long will the workers continue to use cached routing?
[00:07:33] Priya Shah: defaults are conservative — workers cache policies for 5 minutes by default with jitter; for Dedicated we can set longer TTLs or even push a local copy of the routing engine depending on the private control plane configuration.
[00:07:44] Maya Lin: what about testability — can we inject faults and simulate region outages?
[00:07:49] Priya Shah: yes, we provide a chaos harness for pilots — you can simulate worker pool loss, latency spikes, or KV cache eviction and observe automated fallback. We'll coordinate the schedule so you can run tests during safe windows.
[00:07:58] Alex Monroe: note: for hosted we run the chaos harness in a sandbox; for Dedicated/private we can run within your pilot tenancy.
[00:08:05] Carlos Ruiz: do you provide deterministic logs to reconcile which requests were downgraded? we have regulatory audit requirements.
[00:08:12] Priya Shah: yes every downgraded request logs the reason code, preimage hash, model id, target latency, and whether response was served from KV cache. We also provide a reconciliation export for matching request ids.
[00:08:24] Leah Patel: ok sounds good. any known limitations around long-context sequences? we do some transcripts up to 6k tokens.
[00:08:31] Priya Shah: long sequences increase KV cache pressure and amplify decode compute; runtime picks kernels based on sequence length, but for extremely long sequences we recommend segmentation or streaming APIs. We also have quantization profiles that keep quality acceptable for longer contexts.
[00:08:45] Maya Lin: last topic — onboarding and runbook: if we onboard dedicated will your SEs be embedded for the first two weeks?
[00:08:51] Alex Monroe: yes, SE shadowing is standard for Dedicated pilots for up to two weeks; optional extension if you want deeper integration.
[00:08:58] Carlos Ruiz: do you support our SSO (Okta SAML) and RBAC integration?
[00:09:03] Priya Shah: yes Okta SAML is supported, and we map roles to RBAC with granular route/model-level permissions.
[00:09:09] Leah Patel: great. I think that's everything from our side.
[00:09:13] Alex Monroe: recap: Priya will share the pilot plan, Alex will send pricing + contract examples + security pack, Nyx will share traffic profiles and geo rules. any final questions?
[00:09:25] Maya Lin: none. one small nit — you've mentioned model variants by name sometimes and the transcript might show slight misspellings like '8q' vs '8-bit q'. that's fine.
[00:09:36] Alex Monroe: totally fine. we'll follow up via email. thanks everyone.
[00:09:40] Meeting Ended: 00:52:00
